question: How many paths of travel does each traffic lane give a motorcycle, according to the manual?
explanation: Each traffic lane gives a motorcycle three paths of travel, and lane choice should help increase visibility, avoid blind spots and surface hazards, communicate intentions, and provide an escape path.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.16-17, 'Lane Positions'

question: Why does the manual say the center third of the lane can be hazardous?
choice_a: It is illegal to ride there
choice_b: It is always the wettest part of the lane
choice_c: Motorcycles cannot physically fit in the center third
choice_d: Debris and oil drippings from cars collect there, along with hazards such as surface covers
explanation: The center third of the lane is where debris and oil drippings from cars collect and where hazards such as surface covers are located, though unless the road is wet, the typical center strip permits adequate traction.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.17, 'Lane Positions'

question: What is one absolute that experienced riders rely on regarding lane position, according to the manual?
choice_a: Avoid riding in another vehicle's blind spot
choice_b: Always ride in the far right portion of the lane
choice_c: Never change lane position for any reason
choice_d: Always ride in another vehicle's blind spot for cover
explanation: Experienced riders rely on their own strategies and judgment, but one absolute is to avoid riding in another vehicle's blind spot.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.17, 'Lane Positions'

question: What is the minimum following distance that should normally be maintained when following a vehicle?
explanation: "Following too closely" is a frequent factor in crashes involving motorcyclists; normally a minimum of two seconds distance should be maintained when following a vehicle.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.17, 'Following Another Vehicle'

question: How do you gauge your following distance using the marker method?
choice_c: Pick a marker on the road; when the vehicle ahead passes it, count "one-thousand-one, one-thousand-two"; reaching the marker before "two" means you're following too closely
choice_d: Count to ten regardless of speed
explanation: Pick out a marker on or near the road ahead; when the rear of the vehicle ahead passes the marker, count off the seconds -- if you reach the marker before you reach "two," you are following too closely.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.18, 'Following Another Vehicle'

question: When should a rider open up a three-second or more following distance?
choice_b: Following distance should never exceed two seconds under any conditions
choice_d: If the pavement is slippery, visibility through the vehicle ahead is blocked, or traffic is heavy and someone may squeeze in front
explanation: A larger cushion of space -- a three-second or more following distance -- is needed if the pavement is slippery, if you cannot see through the vehicle ahead, or if traffic is heavy and someone may squeeze in front of you.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.18, 'Following Another Vehicle'

question: Where should a rider position themselves in the lane when behind a car, to be seen by the driver?
choice_a: In the center portion of the lane, where the driver can see the rider in the inside rearview mirror
choice_b: Directly in the driver's blind spot
choice_c: As far left as physically possible at all times
choice_d: It doesn't matter, since drivers never check mirrors
explanation: When behind a car, ride where the driver can see you in the inside rearview mirror -- riding in the center portion of the lane should put you in view, since most drivers don't check their sideview mirrors as often as the inside mirror.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.18, 'Following Another Vehicle'

question: What does the manual recommend as a better way to handle a tailgater than speeding up?
choice_a: Speed up as much as possible to lose them
choice_b: Try to get them in front of you by letting them pass, or slow down and open extra space ahead
choice_d: Ignore the situation completely; nothing can be done
explanation: Speeding up to lose a tailgater can result in them tailgating at a higher speed; a better way to handle tailgaters is to get them in front of you by letting them pass, or by slowing down and opening extra space ahead.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.18-19, 'Being Followed'

question: What is the first step listed for passing another vehicle?
choice_a: Immediately move into the oncoming lane without signaling
choice_b: Accelerate hard from the center of the lane without checking mirrors
choice_c: Ride in the left portion of the lane at a safe following distance, signal, and check for oncoming traffic using mirrors and a head check
choice_d: Pass only from the right portion of the lane
explanation: To pass: ride in the left portion of the lane at a safe following distance to increase your line of sight and be more visible, signal, check for oncoming traffic, and use your mirrors and a head check on your blind spot.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.19, 'Passing'

question: According to the manual, what should a rider avoid doing while passing?
choice_a: Signaling before returning to the original lane
choice_b: Checking mirrors before completing the pass
choice_c: Completing the pass within the posted speed limit
choice_d: Lingering in the blind spot of the vehicle being passed
explanation: Don't linger in the blind spot; signal again and complete mirror and head checks before returning to the original lane and canceling the signal. Passes must be completed within posted speed limits and only where permitted.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.19, 'Passing'

question: When being passed from behind, where should a rider stay in the lane?
choice_a: In the center portion of the lane
choice_b: As close to the passing vehicle as possible
choice_c: At the far edge of the lane closest to the passing vehicle
choice_d: It does not matter where a rider positions during a pass
explanation: When being passed from behind, stay in the center portion of your lane -- riding close to the passing vehicle could put you in a hazardous situation.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.19, 'Being Passed'

question: When being passed, why should a rider be cautious of "extended mirrors" on some vehicles?
choice_a: Extended mirrors always fold in automatically for safety
choice_b: Some drivers forget their mirrors hang out farther than their fenders
choice_c: Extended mirrors are illegal and rare
choice_d: They have no effect on passing clearance
explanation: When being passed, watch for extended mirrors -- some drivers forget that their mirrors hang out farther than their fenders, which could result in a collision.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.19-20, 'Being Passed'

question: According to Alabama's motorcycle-specific traffic laws and the manual, is lane sharing (riding between rows of stopped or moving cars in the same lane) generally permitted?
choice_a: Yes, it is encouraged in heavy traffic
choice_c: No -- it is usually prohibited and can leave a rider vulnerable to a hand from a window, a door opening, or a car turning suddenly
choice_d: Lane sharing has no risks at all
explanation: Cars and motorcycles need a full lane to operate safely, so lane sharing is usually prohibited -- riding between rows of stopped or moving cars can leave a rider vulnerable to the unexpected, such as a car door opening or a car turning suddenly.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.20, 'Lane Sharing'

question: When are drivers most tempted to squeeze into a rider's lane, according to the manual?
choice_a: Only late at night on empty roads
choice_b: Drivers never try to squeeze into a motorcycle's lane
choice_c: Only when the motorcycle has its headlight off
choice_d: In heavy, bumper-to-bumper traffic, when they want to pass, when a rider is preparing to turn, or when moving into an exit lane
explanation: Drivers are most tempted to squeeze by a rider in heavy, bumper-to-bumper traffic, when they want to pass, when the rider is preparing to turn at an intersection, or when moving into an exit lane or leaving a highway.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.20, 'Lane Sharing'

question: What should a rider do if a vehicle is merging from an entrance ramp and there is no room to change lanes?
choice_a: Adjust speed to open up space for the merging vehicle
choice_b: Speed up to block the merging vehicle
choice_c: Assume the merging driver has already seen the motorcycle
choice_d: Stop in the lane to force the merging vehicle to wait
explanation: Drivers on an entrance ramp may not see you on the highway; give them plenty of room, changing lanes if possible, or adjusting speed to open up space if there is no room for a lane change.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.20, 'Merging Vehicles'

question: Why does the manual advise against riding next to cars or trucks in other lanes if you don't have to?
choice_a: It is against the law in every state
choice_b: You might be in a blind spot, and a vehicle could switch into your lane without warning, and vehicles in the next lane can block your escape from danger
choice_c: Riding alongside other vehicles improves visibility
choice_d: There is no reason to avoid it
explanation: Do not ride next to cars or trucks in other lanes if you don't have to -- you might be in the blind spot, and a vehicle could switch lanes without warning; vehicles alongside also block your escape path if danger appears in your own lane.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.20, 'Vehicles Alongside'
